chunks.title: The tear drain: anatomy & pump
chunks.tldr: Tears go punctum → canaliculus → sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus. Blinking pumps them through.
points: Puncta: on the back edge of the lid margin, at the medial end where the lashes stop.
Canaliculus: 2 mm down (ampulla), then 8 mm across. Upper and lower join as the common canaliculus in >90%.
Rosenmüller valve: flap where the common canaliculus enters the sac (stops reflux).
Lacrimal sac: 10–12 mm, sits in the fossa between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests.
Nasolacrimal duct: 12–18 mm. Opens into the inferior meatus under the inferior turbinate. Valve of Hasner at the bottom.
Pump: each blink, the orbicularis squeezes the canaliculi and pushes tears down. Opening the eyes creates suction that pulls tears into the sac.
pearls: DCR connects the sac to the middle meatus. The natural duct opens into the inferior meatus.

cards.q: Where does the nasolacrimal duct open?
cards.a: Inferior meatus, below the inferior turbinate (valve of Hasner).

cards.q: Which valve sits at the common canaliculus–sac junction?

chunks.title: Why is the eye watering?
chunks.tldr: Two reasons: too many tears (often from dry eye!) or blocked drainage. Check the punctum first.
points: Hypersecretion: dry eye ('paradoxical watering'), inflammation → gritty, red eye.
Poor drainage: punctal malposition (ectropion), a block anywhere, or pump failure (lax lid, facial palsy).
Drainage problems get worse in cold wind and better in warm dry rooms. Tears running down the cheek → drainage problem.
Punctal problems are the commonest cause: stenosis (very common), ectropion, conjunctivochalasis (loose conjunctival fold), a lash stuck in it, big caruncle.
Pouting punctum = canaliculitis.
Look at the punctum before you probe: dilating it hides stenosis.
Watering in a baby: usually blocked duct, but rule out congenital glaucoma!
chunks.hook: Watery eye? Ask: dry? lid? punctum? duct?

cards.q: Common cause of a watering eye that isn't a blocked drain?

chunks.title: Syringing: hard stop vs soft stop
chunks.tldr: Hard stop = you hit bone → canaliculi are open. Soft stop = blocked before the sac (canalicular).
points: Fluorescein disappearance test: dye should be gone in 5–10 min. Tear meniscus normal 0.2–0.4 mm. ≥0.6 mm = high.
Syringing: dilate the punctum, gently pass the cannula along the canaliculus (pull the lid sideways). Not during acute infection.
Hard stop: cannula hits the medial sac wall and bone → no complete canalicular block.
Hard stop + fluid tasted in the throat = patent (but could still be narrow, or pump failure).
Hard stop + reflux and nothing in the throat = NLD obstruction. The sac swells, reflux comes from both puncta (clear, mucus or pus).
Soft stop: spongy feel. Reflux from the same punctum → that canaliculus is blocked. Reflux from the other punctum → common canaliculus blocked.
Press on the sac and mucus/pus comes back → mucocoele (blocked NLD, open canaliculi).
chunks.hook: Hard = Hit bone = Head's clear (canaliculi OK). Soft = Stuck Sooner.

cards.q: Soft stop with reflux through the upper punctum. Where's the block?
Hard stop, no fluid in the throat, reflux from both puncta?

chunks.title: Jones tests & imaging
chunks.tldr: Jones tests are only for partial blocks (watering, but syringing gets through). DCG = anatomy. Scintigraphy = function.
points: Jones primary: fluorescein in the eye, cotton bud under the inferior turbinate after 5 min. Dye found = system works → hypersecretion. No dye → partial block or pump failure (lots of false negatives).

Jones secondary: wash out the dye, then syringe. Stained fluid in the nose → dye reached the sac → block is in the NLD. Clear fluid → dye never reached the sac → punctum/canaliculus problem or pump failure.
Dacryocystography (DCG): contrast injected → shows the exact block, stones, diverticula. Not during infection.
Scintigraphy: radioactive tears → shows functional blocks in normal conditions.
CT/MRI for sinus or sac tumours. Nasal endoscopy for polyps or a deviated septum.
chunks.hook: Secondary Jones: coloured = Canal (NLD) problem lower down. Clear = upper problem.

cards.a: Drainage is patent → watering is from hypersecretion.

cards.q: Jones secondary: clear saline recovered. Interpretation?
cards.a: Dye didn't enter the sac → upper system (punctum/canaliculus) problem or pump failure.

chunks.title: Punctum & canaliculus problems
chunks.tldr: Narrow punctum → snip punctoplasty. Everted punctum → Ziegler cautery or medial spindle. Hopeless canaliculi → Lester Jones tube.
points: Conjunctivochalasis: loose conjunctival folds over the lower lid. Lubricants or steroids. Surgery: excise the fold or suture it down.
Primary punctal stenosis: blepharitis, idiopathic, herpes, radiation, OCP, long-term glaucoma drops, 5-FU. Treatment: 1-, 2- or 3-snip punctoplasty.
Secondary stenosis (from eversion): retropunctal (Ziegler) cautery, medial conjunctivoplasty (diamond excision), + tarsal strip if the lid is lax.
Canalicular block: trauma, herpes, drugs, radiation. Partial → silicone stent for 6 weeks to 6 months.
Total block → trephination + tube, or join the open part to the sac (needs 6–8 mm of healthy canaliculus).
Worst cases → conjunctivo-DCR with a Lester Jones glass tube from the caruncle to the nose (also for pump failure).
chunks.hook: Lester Jones = a glass bypass when the canaliculi are beyond saving.

cards.q: Name 2 drugs that cause punctal stenosis.

cards.a: Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy with a Lester Jones tube.

chunks.title: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction & DCR
chunks.tldr: Commonest NLDO = idiopathic. Fix = DCR (connect sac to the middle meatus), >90% success.
points: Causes: idiopathic (most), trauma or sinus surgery, GPA (Wegener) and sarcoid, nasopharyngeal tumour.
External DCR: skin cut 10 mm medial to the inner canthus (avoid the angular vein), remove bone, open the sac in an 'H', join sac flaps to nasal mucosa flaps.
Fails because of: small or badly placed ostium, missed common canalicular block, scarring, 'sump syndrome' (bone opening too small and too high).
Risks: scar, bleeding, infection, CSF leak.
Endoscopic DCR: no skin scar, less bleeding, faster. Slightly lower success.
Dacryolith (stone): more common in men. Intermittent watering, firm non-tender sac. Treat with DCR.

cards.q: DCR joins the lacrimal sac to which part of the nose?

cards.a: Bony ostium too small and too high, so the sac doesn't drain fully.

chunks.title: Congenital NLDO & dacryocoele
chunks.tldr: ~20% of newborns have a watery eye. 85% clear by age 1. If not → probe at about 12–18 months.
points: Cause: the valve of Hasner hasn't opened yet (the last part to canalise).
Watering and sticky lashes, worse with colds. Pressing on the sac → mucus comes back.
Check vision and the red reflex. Rule out congenital glaucoma, punctal atresia, conjunctivitis.
Sac massage (block the canaliculus with a finger, roll downward). Antibiotic drops for infection.
Probing: a wire through Hasner's membrane. Delay to 12–24 months if mild. Can repeat. Failure → intubation, balloon, or DCR.
Congenital dacryocoele: bluish swelling below the medial canthal tendon at birth. Big ones can block the nose (breathing trouble). Usually settles, or probe.
Encephalocoele = pulsatile swelling above the medial canthal tendon. Don't confuse them!
chunks.hook: Blue lump below = dacryocoele. Pulsing lump above = brain (encephalocoele).

chunks.title: Canaliculitis & dacryocystitis
chunks.tldr: Canaliculitis = Actinomyces, pouting punctum, sulphur granules. Dacryocystitis = infected sac from a blocked NLD → DCR later.
points: Chronic canaliculitis: Actinomyces israelii (Gram-positive, anaerobic). One-sided sticky eye that doesn't respond to antibiotics.
Red, swollen canaliculus, pus on pressure, pouting punctum, yellow 'sulphur' concretions. The sac is normal.
Antibiotic drops alone rarely work → canaliculotomy + curettage.
Acute canaliculitis → think herpes simplex.
Acute dacryocystitis: painful, tense red lump at the medial canthus ± abscess, preseptal cellulitis. Staph or Strep.
Treat: warm compress + oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav). Don't syringe or probe. Incision risks a fistula. DCR once it settles.
Chronic dacryocystitis: painless mucocoele, pus on pressure → DCR.
Delay intraocular surgery if the tear drainage is infected → risk of endophthalmitis.
chunks.hook: Act-in-omyces lives in the canaliculus. Sulphur = yellow granules.

cards.q: Unilateral chronic mucopurulent conjunctivitis, pouting punctum, yellow granules. Organism?
Should you syringe in acute dacryocystitis?
cards.a: No. Warm compresses + oral antibiotics, then DCR later.
